title: Enzymatic living polymerization for polysaccharide synthesis - Nature
byline: Lin; He; Qi; Wang; Yingxin; Bian; Xinyu; Dong; Xiaoduo; Liu; Yating; Shanshan; Xu; Xiangyun; An; Jieyi; Pan; Xiangcheng; Lee; Myongsoo; Long; Chen; Guosong
html:
Abstract

Polysaccharides have myriad functions throughout biological processes, yet synthetic access to well-defined analogues remains a challenge1,2. Achieving high molecular weight, controlled stereochemistry and sequence precision simultaneously has been elusive using conventional chemical methods that rely on protecting-group manipulations. Here we propose enzymatic living polymerization, which enables the precision preparation of natural polysaccharides with molecular weights up to 660 kg mol−1 but polydispersity from low to less than 1.05. Such a living behaviour originates from the initiator weakly binding with the polymerase, realizing fast equilibrium of the active (bound) and dormant (unbound) species, as demonstrated by mechanistic and computational studies. Our approach is generalizable to diverse polysaccharide types, including sequence-controlled block copolymers, and provides a modular route to explore molecular-weight-dependent biological functions of natural polysaccharides.

Data availability

The data supporting the findings of this study are available in the Article and its Supplementary Information. The RNA-sequencing data generated in this study have been deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus under accession code GSE342464. Molecular-weight characterization data for the polysaccharides studied is available at Figshare (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.34394421)36. More data are available from the corresponding authors upon request. Source data are provided with this paper.

Extended data figures and tables

Schematic illustration and time-dependent HPLC analysis of oligomeric chain-extension products generated during CH3- and TETRA-initiated polymerization over 1–10 min. Stronger-binding CH3 produces a broader series of extension intermediates, whereas weaker-binding TETRA maintains a narrower chain-length distribution, consistent with more uniform chain growth during early propagation.

a, MST binding curves of natural HA oligomers (HA4–HA20) and non-natural initiators (HA-TETRA, TRI, GlcNAcβ-R (GlcNAcβ1-4GlcAβ1-3Galβ1-4Glc), GlcNAcα-R (GlcNAcα1-4GlcAβ1-3Galβ1-4Glc) and HA-TRI) with HAS. b, Corresponding dissociation constants (Kd), spanning the nanomolar to sub-millimolar range. c, NMR T2 relaxation analysis of the strongly binding initiators HA4 and HA6 and the more weakly binding HA-TETRA in the absence and presence of HAS. d, NMR T2 relaxation analysis of HA8, showing minimal T2 shortening upon HAS addition. e, Plots of Mn and Đ as a function of [M0]/[I0], for polymerization initiated by HA8. f, Comparison of Đ obtained with different initiators at [M0]/[I0] = 200. MST and NMR are presented as mean ± s.d. from technical replicate measurements (n = 3 or 4). The error bars in f indicate SEC analysis uncertainty.

a, Schematic illustration of αGP-catalyzed amylose chain extension using α-D-glucose 1-phosphate as the monomer, with inorganic phosphate as the leaving group. b, MST binding curves of the indicated initiators with αGP and the corresponding dissociation constants (Kd). c and d, Plots of Mn and Đ as a function of [M0]/[I0] for polymerization initiated by Mal, Mal3, Mal4, Mal6 and Mal8. e, Comparison of Đ obtained with different initiators at [M0]/[I0] = 500. For iMal4, the Đ value at [M0]/[I0] = 800 was used because of the low signal-to-noise ratio at [M0]/[I0] = 500. MST-derived Kd values are presented as mean ± s.d. from three technical replicate measurements (n = 3). The error bars in e indicate SEC analysis uncertainty.
